title: How to Answer “Tell Me About Yourself” So Employers Want to Hire You
description:
Not sure how to answer “Tell me about yourself” in a job interview? In this video, I’ll show you a simple 3-part formula to answer this common interview question without rambling, reciting your resume, or sounding rehearsed.

You’ll learn how to quickly explain who you are professionally, give employers the receipts that prove your value, and connect your experience directly to the job you’re interviewing for.

Because a strong “Tell me about yourself” answer isn’t your biography. It’s the opening story that helps the interviewer think: This person makes sense for us.

In this video, we’ll cover how to:
- Start your answer with a strong professional headline
- Choose accomplishments that prove your value
- Avoid simply repeating your resume
- Connect your experience to the employer and role
- Keep your answer to about 60–90 seconds
- Make your answer memorable without sounding scripted

If your resume is the part that’s getting you stuck, check out my Get Seen System. It walks you through how to create a stronger, more strategic resume that gets noticed!

transcript: the dreaded tell me about yourself. You want a job, they want a love story. And no, I do not mean you need to gaze across the conference table lovingly and wait for the violence to start. But what I mean is that the interviewer wants to hear a story that makes them think, "Oh, this person, this experience, and this job actually makes sense together, and I want to hand them that final job offer rose." By the way, friends, I'm Kate Kersner, career strategist, 20 years in. I am going to show you how to make that employer love you and offer you the job. Most people answer tell me about yourself by reciting their resume from 2014 on and they lose the interviewer before they get to the juicy good stuff. So do not give them your entire biography. In about 60 to 90 seconds, I want you to show them three things. Who you are professionally, the receipts that prove you are good at it, and why this particular job makes sense as your next chapter. Because the goal here is not to just answer the question. It is to start showing them why you might be the one. So, you want to start with who you are professionally. I don't need to know where you were born, what your favorite hobbies are, or every job you've had since college. Give me the headline. If I ask someone who works with you, "What does this person actually do really well?" What would they say? Maybe it is, I'm a project manager who is really good at bringing messy crossf functional projects under control or I'm an account manager who specializes in growing client relationships and keeping valuable customers from walking out the door. Give me the professional version of you that matters most for this particular job. Then give me the receipts. Do not spend the next minute listing responsibilities because your resume already did that for you. Pick one or two pieces of proof that make your opening statement believable. If you just told me you are great at managing complicated projects, maybe you follow with. In my current role, I managed projects across four department. And last year, I rebuilt our handoff process and reduced missed deadlines by about 30%. Now, I don't just know what you call yourself, I understand why I should believe you. This is also where people make another mistake. They think tell me about yourself means they have to squeeze their entire career into one answer. You absolutely do not. You are not making a documentary. You are making the trailer. So, pick the parts of your experience that make employers want to hear the rest. So far, you have told them who you are and proven it. Now comes the actual love story part. And this is where doing real research before the interview matters. Find something about this company, this role, this mission, this team, or most importantly, the problem this role is trying to solve that genuinely speaks to you. Not the generic, "I love your company culture." nonsense that everyone just pulls off the about page, but find the thing where you think, "Oh, I actually care about that." Maybe their mission statement lines up with something you value. Maybe they are building something you genuinely want to be a part of. Maybe the role lets you do more of the work you are already really good at and actually enjoy. Maybe something about it even makes your little heart go a pitterpatter. Okay, I digress. This is not an actual love story, but this is where you show them why the two of you go together like peanut butter and jelly. You might say that is actually what interests me about this role. I know that your team is focused on improving the customer experience while also scaling operations. And that really caught my attention because that is exactly the kind of work I have enjoyed most in my current role and I'm excited to do more of it. Now the connection is real. You are not saying please hire me because I need a job. You are showing them here's who I am. Here's what I'm great at and here is why what you are building actually makes sense for me. And that little ending changes the entire answer. You are no longer giving them a random collection of facts about you. You are creating a story where your experience leads naturally to their opportunity and suddenly the interviewer can picture how this might actually work. And that is the love story. Notice what you're not saying here. You are not giving them I'm hardworking, passionate, detail oriented, and a people person. Those words are basically interview wallpaper at this point. If you are detail oriented, show me the mistake you caught that saved the company money. If you are great with clients, show me the retention rate you improved. If you are a strong leader, tell me what changed because you led the team and give them something they can remember. Quick side note, if this kind of stuff is helpful, I made you a completely free job search toolkit with more of my job search strategies. I'll drop it below, so grab it and let's keep rolling. Now, let's put the entire answer together. Let's say you're interviewing for a project manager role and they ask, "Tell me about yourself." You could say I'm a project manager who really specializes in taking complicated crossf functional work and making it easier for teams to actually execute. In my current role, I manage projects across four departments. And last year, I rebuilt our handoff process after we were seeing constant delays between teams. Within six months, we reduced missed deadlines by about 30%. And I also led our largest client implementation of the year, which launched two weeks ahead of schedule. What really caught my attention about this particular role was the work your team is doing to scale while keeping the customer experience strong. That combination really speaks to me. It is exactly the kind of work I have been doing and honestly the kind of work I really want to keep doing more of. That answer is not long. It does not sound like you memorized your entire resume in the parking lot. And every part of it is moving the interviewer towards the same conclusion. This person makes sense for us. they really could be the one. You gave them the headline, you gave them the proof, and then you gave them the real reason why this opportunity fits you instead of tacking on some generic, "I've always admired your company." And if you're thinking, "Okay, Kate, I get the strategy, but I need help building the resume that will actually get me these interviews in the first place." That is exactly what my Get Scene guide walks you through step by step. I'll link that below, too. But let's finish this because I want you walking into the interview knowing exactly what to do. Here's the formula I want you to remember. Start with who you are professionally. Give them the receipts and then make the connection to them. Who I am, why should you believe me, and why we make sense together. That is your love story. And it gives the interviewer a much easier path to thinking, "Yep, this is the one for me." And one more thing before you walk into that interview, they already saw your resume and they already know where you've worked and what your job titles were. They chose to spend their time talking to you because something on that resume made them interested. Tell me about yourself is not an invitation to prove you deserve to be in the room because you're already there. It is your first chance to show them why you should be the one walking out with the offer. So the next time they say, "Tell me about yourself." Please do not start with, "Well, I graduated in 2012." Give them the trailer. Give them the receipts and then give them the love story. You want the job and they want to understand why you plus them make sense.
